usage_en:
Used to politely ask for something in a shop, café, or restaurant. Put the item in front of 주세요.

Rule: 주세요 asks for an object. To ask someone to do something, attach -아/어 주세요 to a verb instead (도와주세요).

Used to ask what something is when you don't know its name. Point at it and add 뭐예요?

Rule: 뭐 ends in a vowel, so it always takes 예요, never 이에요.

Used to ask whether something exists or is available. It covers both 'is there' and 'do you have'.

Rule: Use 있어요? for things and places. When asking whether a person is in, 계세요? is the respectful form.

Used to ask the way to a place. Put the destination in front, with no particle needed.

Rule: This asks for the route. To ask which transport to take, use 뭐 타고 가요?

Used to name a place you'd like to visit. The particle 에 is usually dropped in speech.

Rule: -고 싶어요 works only for your own wish. To talk about what someone else wants, use -고 싶어 해요.

Used to ask someone's opinion, or how something is going. Put the topic in front.

Rule: It doubles as a suggestion — 커피 어때요? can mean 'How about coffee?' depending on the situation.

Used to settle on one option when ordering or choosing between things.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 할게요 (김밥으로 할게요). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로 할게요 (커피로 할게요).

Used to ask whether someone has ever had a particular experience.

Rule: Attach -아/어 본 적 있어요? to a verb stem. The natural answer is 있어요 or 없어요 rather than 네 or 아니요.

Used to ask someone for a recommendation. Put the category in front — a food, a place, a show.

Rule: Keep 주세요 on the end. Without it, 추천해요 becomes a statement meaning 'I recommend it'.

Used to make a polite request, noticeably softer than -아/어 주세요.

Rule: Attach -아/어 주실 수 있어요? to a verb stem. 주실 carries an honorific, so it suits strangers and people senior to you.

Used to say what you like or enjoy. Put the thing in front.

Rule: 좋아해요 is a verb and takes 을/를 (한국 음식을 좋아해요). 좋아요 is an adjective and takes 이/가 (한국 음식이 좋아요).

Used when something strikes you as new and wonderful — a common reaction when you first meet a different culture.

Rule: 신기해요 is about novelty and wonder. If you mean something is odd or off, use 이상해요 instead.

Used to ask for a refill or a second helping. In Korean restaurants, side dishes usually come free this way.

Rule: 더 goes right before 주세요, not before the noun — 김치 더 주세요, not 더 김치 주세요.

Used to ask for a discount when haggling.

Rule: This belongs at traditional markets and street stalls. Prices are fixed at department stores and chain shops, so it isn't used there.

Used to ask whether someone has tried out a product.

Rule: 써 보다 is for things you use — cosmetics, apps, tools. For food say 먹어 봤어요?, and for clothes 입어 봤어요?

Used to ask which option the other person prefers.

Rule: 어떤 asks 'which one' among options you can see. 무슨 asks 'what kind' in general.

Used when something turns out different from what you had in mind.

Rule: 생각보다 goes at the front and the adjective follows. Whether it means more or less depends on that adjective — 생각보다 맵지 않아요 means less spicy.

Used to express warmth about everyone being gathered in one place.

Rule: -아/어서 좋아요 attaches any reason to 좋아요 — 날씨가 좋아서 좋아요.

Used to say something has already happened, often to stop someone from doing it again.

Rule: 이미 normally comes with a past-tense verb (이미 먹었어요). 벌써 is close but adds surprise at how soon it happened.

Used for the flutter you feel before something important. It covers both nerves and excitement.

Rule: 떨려요 describes your own feeling and takes no object. To give the cause, put it in front with -아/어서 or -라서 (첫 발표라서 떨려요).

Used to say which country or city you come from.

Rule: 에서 marks a starting point, so it attaches to the place (미국에서 왔어요). Do not use 에, which marks a destination.

A set greeting used when you meet someone you'll be working or studying with. English has no direct equivalent — it asks for their goodwill.

Rule: 부탁드려요 is the humble form of 부탁해요. In formal settings such as an interview or presentation, use 잘 부탁드립니다.

Used to ask where to board a bus, subway line, or shuttle.

Rule: 어디서 marks the place where an action happens. If you only want to know where something is, use 어디예요?

Used to say what you feel like eating.

Rule: -고 싶어요 attaches to a verb stem and speaks only for yourself. For another person's craving, use -고 싶어 해요.

Used to say you cannot eat something, whether because of an allergy, a religion, or your tolerance for spice.

Rule: 못 goes right before the verb and means you are unable to. 안 먹어요 means you choose not to.

Used to ask permission before eating or drinking.

Rule: Attach -아/어도 돼요? to a verb stem. The answer comes back as 네, 돼요 or 아니요, 안 돼요.

Used to ask permission to address someone by a name or title. Koreans often use 언니, 오빠, or 선배 instead of a first name.

Rule: Attach 라고 to a name ending in a vowel (언니라고) and 이라고 to one ending in a consonant (선생님이라고).

literal_en: I want to come here again.
usage_en:
Used to tell someone you enjoyed a place enough to return — a natural compliment to a host or a shop.

Rule: 또 means 'again' and goes before the verb. 다시 is close, but 또 sounds warmer in this phrase.

Used to say which transport you're taking, or to tell someone which one to take.

Rule: 타다 takes 을/를 in writing (버스를 타요), though the particle is usually dropped in speech. The opposite is 내려요.

Used to say which stop or station you're getting off at.

Rule: 에서 marks the place where you get off. Pair it with 타요 for getting on — 2호선 타요, 홍대입구역에서 내려요.

Used to tell a taxi driver where you want to go.

Rule: 까지 marks the end point of the trip. 에 가 주세요 also works, but 까지 sounds more natural to a driver.

Used to ask a restaurant to adjust how your food is prepared.

Rule: Put an adjective stem between 덜 and 게 해 주세요 (덜 맵게 해 주세요). For the opposite, swap 덜 for 더.

literal_en: Can I get a refill of ~?
usage_en:
Used to ask whether something can be refilled. Side dishes, rice, and soup are often free this way in Korea.

Rule: 되다 here means 'is possible'. The answer is 네, 돼요 or 안 돼요.

Used to ask about someone's plans at a certain time.

Rule: 에 attaches to time words like 주말에 and 저녁에, but never to 오늘, 내일, or 어제 — say 내일 뭐 해요?

examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?
What are you doing next week?

usage_en:
Used to invite someone to do something with you. It sounds friendly rather than formal.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을래요 (먹을래요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, use -ㄹ래요 (볼래요?).

literal_en: I think I'll be a little late.
usage_en:
Used to let someone know in advance that you won't arrive on time.

Rule: -을 것 같아요 turns a flat statement into a guess, which sounds softer and more considerate than 늦어요.

Used to tell someone you don't know where you are and need help.

Rule: Korean puts this in the past tense (잃었어요) even though English uses the present. 길을 잃어요 sounds wrong.

Used when giving directions to say the way is simple — no turns needed.

Rule: -으면 돼요 means 'it's enough to ~'. It makes instructions sound easy and reassuring.

Used to tell someone which way to turn when giving directions.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 (오른쪽으로). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로. 돌면 돼요 is just as common as 꺾으면 돼요.

Used to ask whether someone has experienced something before.

Rule: Attach -아/어 봤어요? to a verb stem — 먹어 봤어요?, 가 봤어요?, 입어 봤어요? Without 보다, 봤어요? simply means 'did you see it?'

Used for anything enjoyable — a drama, a class, a person, a trip.

Rule: 재미있어요 covers both 'fun' and 'interesting'. The opposite is 재미없어요, written as one word.

Slang shortened from 강력 추천, meaning a strong recommendation. You'll see it constantly in reviews and casual chat.

Rule: This is casual. With someone senior, or in writing, use 추천해요 or 추천드려요.

Used to ask about the weather at a place or on a certain day.

Rule: Put the place or time straight in front, with no particle — 서울 날씨 어때요?, 내일 날씨 어때요?

Used to guess that rain or snow is on the way, based on what you can see.

Rule: In everyday Korean, rain and snow 오다 rather than 내리다 — 비 와요, 눈 와요.

examples.en: It looks like it's going to snow.
It looks like it's going to rain.
It looks like a shower is coming soon.
